subject: Automotive & EVs
title: Why Batteries Degrade Over Time
description: A micro-lesson that makes Why Batteries Degrade Over Time usable.

hook.text: Every time you charge and discharge a battery, it loses a tiny bit of its original capacity.

buildup.text: Chemical side reactions slowly build up deposits inside the cell, blocking the flow of ions.

discovery.text: After hundreds of cycles, these deposits reduce how much energy the battery can hold—this is degradation.

twist.text: Heat is degradation's worst enemy—a battery kept cool degrades far slower than one that runs hot.

climax.text: Most modern EVs retain over 80 percent of battery capacity after 200,000 miles of real-world driving.

punchline.text: EV batteries age, but much slower than most people fear.

quiz.question: What accelerates battery degradation the most?

details.summary: EV batteries slowly lose capacity over thousands of charge cycles as chemical side reactions consume active lithium, grow resistive layers on electrodes, and cause microscopic structural damage.
details.whyItMatters: Battery degradation determines how long an EV remains useful and affects resale value. Modern cells retain 80 to 90 percent capacity after 200,000 miles, far longer than many owners expected.
takeaways: Side reactions form a growing film that traps active lithium
Heat and frequent fast charging accelerate degradation rates
Most modern EVs retain over 80 percent capacity after 150,000 miles

faq.question: What is the biggest factor that accelerates battery degradation?
faq.answer: Heat is the primary enemy. Batteries stored or operated at high temperatures degrade significantly faster. Keeping the battery cool through thermal management and moderate charging preserves longevity.

faq.question: Do EV manufacturers offer battery warranties against degradation?
faq.answer: Most manufacturers warranty the battery for 8 years or 100,000 miles, guaranteeing at least 70 percent capacity retention. Some brands like Tesla cover up to 150,000 miles on certain models.
